plan.topic: Loose stools the morning after Thanksgiving dinner on tirzepatide: what the label says about diarrhea, fluids and when to call
plan.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide and Diarrhea After a Big Holiday Meal: When to Call #shorts'. Sentence 1 (14 words or fewer): 'On tirzepatide, diarrhea is a common side effect listed on the label.' Then the 15 mg vs placebo card with the population, and the exact PI sentence on dose escalation. Then the guilt-free fluid and pharmacist tips, the call-your-prescriber dehydration signs, the exact emergency card, the don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.', and the loop line.
plan.why: It's Thanksgiving Day, and holiday felt-symptom Shorts are proven (full the morning after 495, stuffing 329). This symptom hasn't been used as a holiday angle yet. | fact-check: Diarrhea is a common adverse reaction in Zepbound PI Table 2 (about 23% at 15 mg vs about 7% on placebo). Confirm the exact figures in the current label (accessdata 217806 2026 revision or DailyMed) and show both groups plus the population on screen. Two fixes: (1) The angle paraphrases the label as 'mostly during dose escalation'. The source wording is 'The majority of reports/events of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time.' Copy the current PI sentence word for word. Don't rewrite it as 'mostly', and don't add 'so'. (2) The Thanksgiving framing must not say the meal caused the diarrhea, and must not shame the eating. Present the holiday only as the setting ('if it happens after a big holiday meal'). Fluid tip: keep 'unless you've been told to limit fluids'. Anti-diarrhea products: ask a pharmacist or prescriber first. Dehydration line: keep the label's link between fluid loss and kidney problems as 'can lead to', not 'causes'. Emergency card: use the Medication Guide wording exactly ('severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without vomiting', then stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away). Follow it with the full two-card don't-stop line. Tight arm: 90–120 words.

package.title: Tirzepatide Diarrhea: How Common Is It? (Holiday Meal Edition) #shorts
package.description:
Diarrhea on tirzepatide is a common adverse reaction. In weight-loss trials, about 23 in 100 on tirzepatide 15 mg had it vs about 8 in 100 on placebo. The label says the majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time.
Sip fluids, unless you've been told to limit fluids. Before anti-diarrhea products, ask a pharmacist or prescriber. Peeing less than usual, or dizzy? Call your prescriber.
If you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting, stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away.
For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
#Tirzepatide
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.hook_pattern: negation: 'Diarrhea on tirzepatide is not rare: it is a common adverse reaction.' (12 words. It names the drug and the felt symptom. Sentence 2 gives 23 in 100 vs 8 in 100 on placebo.) Spoken word count: 158 (s1 12, s2 30, s3 22, s4 17, s5 23, s6 30, s7 16, s8 8), inside the standard arm of 135–160. Watch-next target (Exp G): holiday → Thanksgiving long video. Packaging uses the generic name 'tirzepatide' only, with no #Mounjaro and no Mounjaro rates, because the numbers come from the Zepbound label. Emergency line for the caption and post notes, matching the Medication Guide (Revised 11/2026): 'Stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting.' Then the full don't-stop line: 'For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.'

factcheck.summary:
I checked every claim against the current Zepbound label on DailyMed (revised November 16, 2026), the DailyMed Medication Guide (Revised 11/2026) and the NHS dehydration page (last reviewed 01 May 2026). Everything matches the sources.

- **Diarrhea rates:** Table 1 gives 23% on 15 mg vs 8% on placebo, from the pool of 2 weight-reduction trials (2,519 adults, up to 72 weeks).
- **s3 quote:** the dose-escalation sentence is word for word from section 6.1.
- **s6 emergency line:** the current Medication Guide now reads "with or without nausea or vomiting". The craft note's "with or without vomiting" for tirzepatide is out of date for this label, so s6 is correct.
- **s5:** the dehydration and kidney sentence matches the Medication Guide, and "peeing less often than usual" and "feeling dizzy or lightheaded" are on the NHS list.

**Word count:** I counted it myself and got 158 (12/30/22/17/23/30/16/8), inside the 135–160 standard arm. The fixed safety lines are copied exactly, the fluid caveat is there, there are no digits in the narration, and there's no dosing or stop/switch advice.

**Sources:** the Lilly Medication Guide PDF (S2) loads but its text couldn't be read, so its 11/2026 date comes from the DailyMed copy (S2b). That copy says the same thing.

Only small wording fixes remain (listed below).

issues.claim: Diarrhea, tirzepatide 15 mg vs placebo, over 72 weeks
issues.problem: The label describes the pool as patients treated 'for up to 72 weeks' (plus a 4-week follow-up off the drug), not 'over 72 weeks'.
issues.fix: stat_label: "Diarrhea, tirzepatide 15 mg vs placebo, trials up to 72 weeks"; in the attribution, replace "72 weeks" with "up to 72 weeks".

issues.claim: 23% on tirzepatide 15 mg vs 8% on placebo
issues.problem: This fails the muted-viewer test: the card doesn't name the measure (diarrhea) or the population, so a viewer without sound sees a number with no subject.
issues.fix: on_screen_text: "Diarrhea: 23% on tirzepatide 15 mg vs 8% on placebo (weight-loss trials, adults)"

issues.claim: Tirzepatide and Diarrhea After a Holiday Meal: When to Call
issues.problem: The title links the diarrhea to the holiday meal, but the script says the holiday is only the setting, never the cause. Viewers may read it as 'holiday food triggers it'.
issues.fix: "Diarrhea on Tirzepatide Over the Holidays: How Common It Is and When to Call #shorts"

issues.problem: 'Diarrhea After Thanksgiving' could suggest that the 23% figure, or the diarrhea itself, is tied to Thanksgiving meals. The script only says a holiday meal can make it feel embarrassing. It makes no claim about timing or cause, and the trial data has nothing holiday-specific. This is a wording issue, not a false claim.
